flawed_step: Step 4: regularity does not imply that an automorphism exchanges the two endpoint-orbits.
counterexample: Let P=(Z/3Z)^3 and let L consist of symbols X_{b,c}, Y_{a,c}, Z_{a,b}. Join (a,b,c) to X_{b,c}, Y_{a,c}, and Z_{a,b}. This is a finite simple 3-regular edge-transitive graph, but point vertices and line vertices have different distance distributions, so it is not vertex-transitive.
assessment_summary:
1. [Justified] If a regular graph has no edges, every vertex is isolated, so every permutation of its vertices is an automorphism; hence it is vertex-transitive.
2. [Justified] Now assume the graph has an edge {u,v}. Every vertex x has positive degree, so choose an incident edge {x,y}. Edge-transitivity supplies an automorphism sending {x,y} to {u,v}; thus x is sent to either u or v. Consequently there are at most two vertex-orbits.
3. [Justified] If there are two vertex-orbits A and B, every edge has one endpoint in each: the endpoints of a fixed edge represent the two orbits, and edge-transitivity preserves this endpoint-orbit pattern.
4. [Unjustified] A purported proof would now claim that regularity forces an automorphism interchanging A and B. Regularity only gives |A|d=|B|d and hence |A|=|B|; equal orbit sizes do not produce such an automorphism. This is the first failing step.
5. [Unjustified] Therefore the proposed conclusion that the graph must have one vertex-orbit does not follow from Steps 1–4.
6. [Justified] To show the statement itself is false, define a bipartite graph H with point part P=(Z/3Z)^3 and line part L={X_{b,c},Y_{a,c},Z_{a,b}:a,b,c in Z/3Z}, where (a,b,c) is adjacent exactly to X_{b,c}, Y_{a,c}, and Z_{a,b}.
7. [Justified] H is finite and simple. Every point has its three displayed neighbors, while each line symbol has the three points obtained by varying its omitted coordinate; hence H is 3-regular.
8. [Justified] H is edge-transitive. Permuting the three coordinates permutes the line directions X,Y,Z, and independently permuting the three values in each coordinate gives automorphisms. Given two incident point-line pairs, these permutations can first match their directions and then match all three point coordinates, carrying one edge to the other.
9. [Justified] From a point p, a point differing from p in k coordinates is at distance 2k. Thus the numbers of vertices at distances 0,2,4,6 are respectively 1,6,12,8; in particular, exactly 12 vertices are at distance 4 from p.
10. [Justified] From the line vertex X_{0,0}, the line vertices occur at even distances with counts 1 at distance 0, 6 at distance 2, 16 at distance 4, and 4 at distance 6. Indeed, the six distance-2 lines intersect X_{0,0}; the sixteen distance-4 lines comprise four other X-lines with exactly one nonzero index, six Y-lines with nonzero second index, and six Z-lines with nonzero second index; the remaining four X-lines are at distance 6.
11. [Justified] Graph automorphisms preserve distances and therefore preserve the number of vertices at each distance. Since a point has 12 vertices at distance 4 while a line vertex has 16, no automorphism maps a point to a line vertex.
12. [Justified] H is consequently regular and edge-transitive by Steps 7–8 but not vertex-transitive by Step 11. It is a counterexample, so the stated universal claim is false.
